newsitem.title: GERMANY: MOTORCYCLING-KENNY'S NEW TOY KEEPS IMPROVING.
newsitem.headline: MOTORCYCLING-KENNY'S NEW TOY KEEPS IMPROVING.

text.p: Kenny Roberts's faith in a former motocross rider and a home-made bike in this year's 500cc motorcycle world championship started to pay dividends at Nuerburgring on Saturday.

Both France's Jean-Michel Bayle and his machine, the Roberts-built and Malaysian-funded Modenas KR V3, proved they could mix it with the best after qualifying fifth-fastest in final practice for Sunday's German Grand Prix.

That was the best qualifying time so far for the new prototype, whose engine is built in Britain with the rest of the bike put together by Roberts, if perhaps slightly disappointing for Bayle who was briefly second-fastest.
The Frenchman, who crashed twice in the session, was looking set for a front-row slot when he was knocked down to fifth place in the dying minutes by Italian Luca Cadalora on a Yamaha.

But the former 250cc motocross world champion, who clinched his first career 500cc pole on a Team Roberts Yamaha last season, was still delighted at the idea of starting his new toy from the second row for the first time.
"Maybe I was pushing a little too hard," he said. "My thanks to the team, who've had a lot of work to do with my two crashes. But I'm trying my best to make them happy."
Bayle rode the bike for the first time in January but has taken it into the points in four races since then.
Roberts, who himself won the 500cc title three times, has been a team manager for the last 10 years, winning three 500cc titles with Wayne Rainey from 1990 to 1992.
Looking for a fresh challenge, he last year hired Bayle, who had enjoyed little success with Aprilia in the 250cc category and had no experience at all in the 500cc class.

He took even more of a gamble this year by using the British Formula One industry and Malaysian money to launch a bizarre-looking bike with a three-cylinder engine designed in association with Tom Walkinshaw, boss of the Arrows motor racing team.

The bike had considerable problems early in the season, which Roberts admitted would focus more on development rather than immediately taking on the mighty Japanese constructors, who have captured every 500cc title since 1973.
Australian triple world champion Michael Doohan felt the same way, welcoming Roberts's initiative earlier in the year but saying he wanted to race bikes rather than develop them.
On Saturday, however, it became apparent that the Modenas can no longer be written off as a contender.
"It's getting better," said a proud Roberts. "The performance level is coming up and we're learning as we go."
Roberts was confident Bayle would improve on the team's best race results so far, two eighth places in Mugello and Imola.

"I think Jean-Michel will be able to race with the front guys tomorrow (Sunday)," he said. "If you look at the time sheets there'a lot of four cylinders behind us and they've been racing those bikes for years."
The Modenas, particularly at ease on the twisty German circuit, where sheer performance matters less than elsewhere, still has a few problems to solve in terms of reliability.
The team's second rider, Roberts's eldest son Kenny Roberts Junior, found that to his cost on Saturday as he spent most of the session in the pits because of engine failure on both his bikes.
"We still have a problem with Junior's bikes though," acknowledged Roberts. "But we are learning fast and we'll improve even more as we put what we learn into practice."
